# Code review iteration

Full read-through of kamilsk/dotfiles at commit `5662ea4 2025-11-20`: the `install` bootstrap, `bin/` scripts and `bin/lib/` shell libraries, `config/` rc files, `test/` bats suite, `toolset/` (Brewfiles, Go tools module), `Makefile`, `Taskfile`, and `.github/` bot configs. Review angle: shell correctness and safety (quoting, error handling, bash-vs-zsh semantics), macOS portability, secrets hygiene, bootstrap reproducibility, and currency of tooling against 2026 practice. `.github/issues/` and `.github/roadmap/` were excluded as offline backlog dumps. No previous review files existed in `.github/reviews/`, so nothing was matched against. Key shell-semantics claims (top-level `return` under `set -e`, zsh `path` tie) were verified in isolated throwaway shells, not by running repo code.

Class: `correctness` · `security` · `concurrency` · `perf` · `api` · `idiom` · `modern` · `test` · `build` · `docs`.

## 1. Top-level return aborts the installer instead of exiting gracefully

Anchor: install:130.

```bash
install-clt
if ! check; then return 0; fi
```

`install` is executed, not sourced (`bash -c "$(curl ...)"`), so `return` at the top level of the script is illegal. When `check` fails (git or curl missing — exactly the situation this guard exists for), bash prints `return: can only 'return' from a function or sourced script` and, because of `set -euo pipefail` at install:3, the script dies with exit code 2. Verified in an isolated shell: the graceful-exit path never executes and instead produces a confusing error on precisely the machines that need the friendly message most.

**Fix.** Replace `return 0` with `exit 0` (or `exit 1` — arguably a missing prerequisite is a failure, not success). While here, note that `install-clt` runs *before* `check`, so the CLT install message can appear on a machine that is about to bail out anyway; run `check` first.

## 2. Every install run ends in failure because compaudit is not a bash command

Anchor: install:144.

```bash
compaudit | xargs chmod g-w,o-w # todo: not tested in the whole installation process
```

`compaudit` is a zsh function autoloaded by `compinit`; it does not exist in bash at all, and it would not exist even in a non-interactive zsh that has not run `compinit`. In this bash script the line fails with `command not found`, and since it is executed under `set -euo pipefail` as the final statement, **every** run of the advertised one-liner install terminates with a non-zero exit and an error message — even when everything else succeeded. The `todo` comment admits this was never tested end-to-end.

**Fix.** Run it through zsh explicitly and tolerate absence: `zsh -ic 'compaudit' 2>/dev/null | xargs chmod g-w,o-w || true` — or drop the line entirely, since install:59 (`chmod -R go-w "$(brew --prefix)/share/zsh"`) already covers the common Homebrew case.

## 3. Xcode CLT detection never triggers because xcode-select always exists

Anchor: install:34-38.

```bash
install-clt() {
  if [[ ! "$(uname)" =~ Darwin ]]; then return 0; fi
  if command -v xcode-select >/dev/null; then return 0; fi
  echo Installing Command Line Tools for Xcode...
  xcode-select --install
```

The `xcode-select` binary ships with macOS itself and is present whether or not the Command Line Tools are installed. `command -v xcode-select` therefore always succeeds on Darwin, the function always returns early, and the CLT are never installed — yet the very next steps (`git clone`, Homebrew) hard-depend on them. On a truly fresh machine the bootstrap fails at `check` (see finding 1) instead of installing its own prerequisite. Additionally, `xcode-select --install` merely pops an async GUI dialog and returns immediately, so even if the branch were reached, the script would race ahead of the actual installation.

**Fix.** Test for the tools, not the shim: `if xcode-select -p >/dev/null 2>&1; then return 0; fi`. After triggering `--install`, poll until `xcode-select -p` succeeds (e.g. `until xcode-select -p >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 5; done`) before proceeding.

## 4. Fresh-machine bootstrap requires SSH keys and a TTY it does not have

Anchor: install:46, install:90-91, .gitmodules:2.

```bash
git clone --recurse-submodules git@github.com:kamilsk/dotfiles.git "${root}"
...
open "https://getoutline.org/get-started/#step-3"
read -r -p "Please install and configure VPN, and press Enter to continue"
```

Three independent problems break the advertised `curl -sSfL ... | bash` flow on a clean machine:

1. The clone uses the SSH remote, and all four submodules in `.gitmodules` also use `git@github.com:` URLs. A fresh machine has no GitHub SSH key yet, so the clone (and any later `git submodule update --init`) fails with `Permission denied (publickey)`. This is a public repo with public submodules — HTTPS works anonymously.
2. In the piped variant (`curl ... | bash`), stdin *is* the script, so `read -r -p` at install:91 either consumes script text as its input or fails outright; the interactive pause only works in the `bash -c "$(curl ...)"` variant. An installer must not assume a TTY on stdin.
3. `install-vpn` runs `open` unconditionally, while its siblings carefully guard on Darwin — on Linux (which `install-homebrew` explicitly supports via linuxbrew) this kills the script under `set -e`.

**Fix.** Clone via `https://github.com/kamilsk/dotfiles.git` and switch `.gitmodules` URLs to HTTPS (use `insteadOf` locally if you prefer pushing over SSH). Read prompts from the terminal explicitly (`read -r -p ... </dev/tty`) or make the VPN step opt-in/non-interactive, and gate it on Darwin like the other steps.

## 5. touch_sudo writes a root PAM config through a predictable tmp path

Anchor: bin/lib/mac.bash:16-24.

```bash
echo '# sudo: auth account password session' >/tmp/sudo
echo 'auth       sufficient     pam_tid.so' >>/tmp/sudo
cat </etc/pam.d/sudo | grep -v '# sudo' >>/tmp/sudo
sudo mv /tmp/sudo /etc/pam.d/sudo
```

The staging file lives at a fixed, predictable path in world-writable `/tmp`. A local attacker can pre-create `/tmp/sudo` (mode 0666, owned by them): your `>` redirection then writes into *their* file, they keep ownership and an open descriptor, and they can rewrite the contents in the window before `sudo mv` installs it as root into `/etc/pam.d/sudo` — i.e. attacker-controlled PAM auth policy for sudo, a classic TOCTOU privilege escalation. Independent of the race, editing `/etc/pam.d/sudo` directly is the outdated approach: macOS overwrites that file on every OS update (silently removing your `pam_tid.so` line), which is why macOS 14 Sonoma introduced `/etc/pam.d/sudo_local` precisely for this TouchID snippet.

**Fix.** Stage via `tmp=$(mktemp)` and write `/etc/pam.d/sudo_local` instead of `sudo`:

```bash
sudo cp /etc/pam.d/sudo_local.template /etc/pam.d/sudo_local  # then uncomment pam_tid.so
```

On Sonoma+ that is two lines, survives OS updates, and never touches a shared tmp path.

## 6. The path helper clobbers PATH for the whole zsh session

Anchor: bin/lib/env.bash:39 (also 30).

```bash
has)
  shift
  for path in "${@}"; do
```

These `.bash` libraries are sourced into zsh by `config/zsh/.zshrc:26-28`. In zsh, `path` is a special array parameter tied to `PATH`. The loop variable is not declared local, so `for path in "${@}"` assigns each argument to the tied parameter — verified: after calling `path has /usr/bin`, `PATH` is literally `/usr/bin` for the rest of the session and every other command disappears (`command -v ls` fails). The diagnostic helper destroys the very thing it inspects. The sibling loop variable `arg` at env.bash:30 likewise leaks into the interactive shell's global namespace, and naming the function itself `path` shadows zsh's tied array in scripts that treat it as such.

**Fix.** Rename the loop variable (`for candidate in "$@"`) and declare loop variables `local` inside functions. Consider renaming the function (e.g. `paths`) to stop colliding with zsh's `path` parameter entirely. If the dual bash/zsh sourcing stays, add a smoke test that sources every `bin/lib/*.bash` under `zsh -f` and asserts `PATH` is intact.

## 7. Repo-wide staleness across bots, CI, Go tooling, and vendored installers

Anchor: .github/stale.yml:1 (representative; details below).

The repo's automation and toolchain choices are consistently 2020-era. One consolidated list with a migration outline:

- **No CI at all.** There is no `.github/workflows/`; nothing runs shellcheck, shfmt, or the bats suite. For a repo that is 90% shell, a single lint+test workflow would have caught findings 1, 2, and 13 mechanically.
- **Dead probot apps.** `.github/stale.yml` targets probot/stale, which is archived — the config even links its own deprecation issue and names the replacement (`actions/stale`). `.github/settings.yml` targets the probot settings app, long in maintenance mode; GitHub-native repository rulesets now cover most of it.
- **Unpinned third-party curl installs.** `Makefile:18` and `Makefile:32` download executables from `raw.github.com` (the pre-2014 redirect host) at `master`, into `bin/` which is on `PATH` — the SHA check compares the latest upstream commit but then fetches unpinned `master` anyway, so you execute whatever upstream (or a compromised upstream) pushes. `install:115` does the same for oh-my-zsh via `raw.github.com`. Pin by commit SHA on `raw.githubusercontent.com`, or vendor the files outright.
- **Dead self-update protocol in vendored script.** `bin/spot:63` clones `git://github.com/...` — GitHub disabled the git protocol in March 2022, so `spot -U` can never work again.
- **Go tools module predates the tool directive.** `toolset/go.mod:3` already declares `go 1.25.0`, but `toolset/tools.go` still uses the blank-import + `//go:generate go install` pattern. Go 1.24+ replaces this wholesale with `tool` directives (`go get -tool <pkg>`, `go tool <name>`), removing the build tag, the generate step, and the Makefile glue.
- **Archived/deprecated tools in the toolset.** `github.com/golang/mock` (toolset/go.mod:9) was archived in 2023 — successor is `go.uber.org/mock`. `golang.org/x/tools/cmd/gorename` is pinned at `v0.1.0-deprecated` (toolset/go.mod:20), and `benchcmp` (toolset/tools.go:20) is deprecated in favor of `benchstat`. `spaghetti` and `x/exp` are pinned to 2021/2025 pseudo-versions worth revisiting.
- **Archived fonts submodule.** The `fonts` submodule tracks powerline/fonts, archived upstream in 2024; the current ecosystem answer (for the agnoster/powerline glyph setup in `.zshrc`) is Nerd Fonts via Homebrew casks — no submodule needed.

**Fix.** Migration order: (1) add one GitHub Actions workflow running shellcheck + shfmt + bats and a `dependabot.yml` entry for `github-actions`; (2) delete `stale.yml` or move to `actions/stale`, decide consciously whether `settings.yml` still has a live app behind it; (3) convert `toolset` to `go get -tool` and drop `tools.go`; swap mock→uber-go/mock, benchcmp→benchstat, drop gorename; (4) pin or vendor the Makefile-curled scripts; (5) replace the fonts submodule with a `font-*-nerd-font` cask in the Brewfile.

## 8. self-update evals unvalidated arguments and hard-resets the work tree

Anchor: bin/self-update:109, 116, 119.

```bash
*)
  UPDATE+=("echo unknown type: ${type}")
  ;;
...
for update in "${UPDATE[@]}"; do
  eval "${update}"
done
...
(cd "${root}" && git reset --hard) # clean up
```

Unknown CLI arguments are interpolated verbatim into a string that is later `eval`ed: `self-update 'x; rm -rf ~/something'` executes the payload. It is self-inflicted (own argv), but the `eval` buys nothing — every other array element is a bare function name. Separately, the unconditional `git reset --hard` at bin/self-update:119 silently destroys any local uncommitted changes in `~/.dotfiles` every time `self-update` runs; combined with `update_dotfiles` already doing `git pull --rebase`, this is a data-loss footgun rather than "clean up".

**Fix.** Store only function names in `UPDATE`, invoke them as `"${update}"` (no `eval`), and handle unknown types with `echo "unknown type: ${type}" >&2; exit 1` at parse time. Replace `git reset --hard` with a dirty-tree check that warns and aborts (`git diff --quiet || { echo 'local changes present'; exit 1; }`).

## 9. git-pull defers the stash pop to shell exit in bash

Anchor: bin/lib/git/sync.bash:4-7 (same code inlined at bin/lib/git.bash:70-74).

```bash
git-pull() {
  if ! git diff-index --quiet HEAD; then
    git stash -m 'stash before pull'
    trap '{ git stash pop; }' EXIT
  fi
```

This function is sourced into interactive shells for both bash and zsh. The two shells disagree about what `trap ... EXIT` inside a function means: zsh runs the trap when the *function* returns; bash runs it when the *shell* exits. So under bash (`config/bash/.bash_profile` sources the same file), `pull` stashes your dirty changes and then leaves them stashed for the entire session — the pop fires hours later when you close the terminal, in whatever directory/branch you happen to be in then, silently applying old changes or spawning conflicts. It also overwrites any EXIT trap the user had. Even in zsh, the trap fires on *any* exit path, popping the stash onto a half-rebased tree when the pull fails midway.

**Fix.** Git already solves this race-free: `git pull --rebase --autostash` (and `git rebase --autostash`), available since git 2.9/2.27. Drop the manual stash/trap dance entirely; if manual control is preferred, pop explicitly after a successful pull instead of via trap.

## 10. The dependency updater dies at startup when go, npm, or composer is missing

Anchor: bin/update:5-7.

```bash
set -euo pipefail

__go=$(which go)
__npm=$(which npm)
__php=$(which composer)
```

Under `set -e`, an assignment's exit status is that of its command substitution, so the very first missing tool kills the whole script: on a machine without composer, `update go` — which needs no PHP at all — fails at line 7 before doing anything. The three lookups are eager but only one is ever needed per invocation. (The `which`-capture exists so the `go`/`npm`/`php` *functions* can call the real binaries — a fine trick, but it must not make each runtime a hard prerequisite of the others. Secondary nit: `__check`'s `trap ... EXIT` at bin/update:11 prints "please stash or commit changes" for *any* later non-zero exit, misattributing unrelated failures.)

**Fix.** Resolve lazily and tolerantly: `__go=$(command -v go || true)` then guard inside each function (`[ -n "${__go}" ] || { echo 'go not installed' >&2; return 1; }`). Prefer `command -v` over `which` throughout — it is POSIX, builtin, and shellcheck-clean. Scope the check trap to the failure it describes.

## 11. Malformed character class breaks release tag selection

Anchor: bin/git_current:34 and 37.

```bash
if git tag --points-at "${latest}" | grep -v '[:alpha:]' >/dev/null; then
```

Outside double brackets, `[:alpha:]` is not the alphabetic class — it is a plain bracket expression matching the five characters `a l p h :` (GNU grep even warns about exactly this). The intent (per the comment: pick the numeric tag among `vX.Y.Z`, `X.Y.Z`, `latest`) is to filter out tags containing letters, but the actual filter keeps `v1.2.3` (no `a/l/p/h/:` in it) and only excludes `latest` by coincidence of its spelling. Any tag like `beta-1` or `v2.0.0-rc.1` slips through or is dropped on the wrong criterion, so the `git release`/`git state` aliases report the wrong tag.

**Fix.** Use the real class: `grep -v '[[:alpha:]]'` — or express the intent positively and more strictly: `git tag --points-at "${latest}" | grep -E '^[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)*$'` with a fallback to the raw `git describe` output when nothing matches.

## 12. The hand-rolled include preprocessor has already drifted from its sources

Anchor: bin/lib/git.bash:21 vs bin/lib/git/commit.bash:22; bin/lib/sys.bash:3-88; bin/lib/sys/sign-in.bash:1.

```bash
# bin/lib/git.bash (the copy that is actually sourced)
GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="${_cd}" git commit --amend --date="${_ad}" --no-edit ${1+"${@}"}
# bin/lib/git/commit.bash (the nominal source of truth)
GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="${_cd}" git commit --amend --date="${_ad}" --no-edit "${@}"
```

`bin/lib/git.bash` and `bin/lib/sys.bash` are stitched-together copies of the files under `bin/lib/git/` and `bin/lib/sys/`, marked with `#include:...|uncomment` pragmas for a preprocessor that is not in the repo. The rc files source only the top-level `*.bash`, so the *copies* are what actually runs — and they have already diverged: `git-amend` uses the archaic `${1+"${@}"}` (a pre-POSIX workaround obsolete in every bash/zsh this repo targets) while the source file was modernized to `"${@}"`; all doc comments were stripped from the copies. Meanwhile `bin/lib/sys/sign-in.bash` is included by nothing and sourced by nothing — dead code that looks alive.

**Fix.** Pick one mechanism. Simplest: delete the generated blocks and source the subdirectories directly (`for script in "${DOT}"/bin/lib/**/*.bash`), or keep the flat files and delete the subdirectory duplicates. If generation must stay, commit the generator, add a CI check that regeneration is clean, and wire `sign-in.bash` in or remove it.

## 13. The test suite asserts scripts and aliases that no longer exist

Anchor: test/lookup.bats:28-29 (also 16, 22, 51-59); test/datetime.bats:4, 28.

```bash
assert_output --partial 'git alias: !git_commit cmm'
assert_output --partial 'bin/git_commit: Bourne-Again shell script text executable'
```

The bats suite tests a repo that no longer exists: there is no `bin/git_commit`, no `bin/explain`, no `bin/git_aliases` (it now lives only as a reference in `bin/legacy/git`), and `git_config` sets `alias.cmm` to `'!@ git-commit'`, not `'!git_commit cmm'`; nothing sets `alias.m` to `checkout master` anymore. Every one of these tests fails against the current tree. `test/datetime.bats` is worse in a different way: it defines its own private copy of `datetime` (test/datetime.bats:4, the `TODO:deprecated` admits it) rather than loading `bin/lib/helpers.bash`, and its single test — `run datetime -1d1H` — contains no assertion at all, so it passes vacuously no matter what the function does. Net test coverage of the real code is zero, which is how findings 1, 2, and 11 survived.

**Fix.** Point the suite at the shipped code: `load` the actual `bin/lib/*.bash` (or exercise `bin/@`), update expectations to the current aliases, add assertions to datetime tests (`assert_success` + output shape), and run bats in the CI workflow from finding 7 so the suite cannot rot silently again.

## 14. sudo pip and sudo gem global upgrades are a pre-PEP-668 idiom

Anchor: bin/lib/aliases.bash:44-45, 52-55 (also 39-40).

```bash
alias gem+='sudo gem update --system; \
            gem list | cut -d" " -f1 | xargs -n1 sudo gem update'
...
alias pip+='pip list | cut -d" " -f1 | xargs -n1 sudo pip install --upgrade'
```

Blanket `sudo pip install --upgrade` of every listed package writes into the interpreter's system site-packages as root. On 2026 systems this is not just frowned upon, it is actively rejected: Homebrew/Debian Pythons are PEP 668 "externally managed" and pip refuses without `--break-system-packages` (which is exactly what it would do). `sudo gem update --system` against macOS system Ruby is similarly deprecated territory. The `pip+` parsing (`cut -d" " -f1` without `tail -n +3`) also chokes on pip's two header lines — its `pip3+` twin got the `tail` but this branch never did. These aliases date from the era before pipx/uv and language-version managers.

**Fix.** Drop `sudo` everywhere here. For CLI tools, `pipx upgrade-all` or `uv tool upgrade --all`; for library environments, per-project virtualenvs (the repo already has `v@`/`v+` aliases for exactly that); for Ruby, a user-level install via rbenv/mise. If the aliases stay, use `pip list --format=freeze | cut -d= -f1` instead of column-slicing human output.

## 15. datetime evals unsanitized input and only works with BSD date

Anchor: bin/lib/helpers.bash:64-70 (also 40).

```bash
local v
for m in $(echo "${mutator}" | cat); do
  v+="-v${sign}${m} "
done
eval "date -j ${v}+'${iso}'"
```

The argument reaches `eval` after only a cosmetic sed pass, so shell metacharacters in it are executed: `datetime '1d$(touch /tmp/pwned)'` runs the substitution. The blast radius grows because `git-at` (bin/lib/git/commit.bash:4) pipes its first argument straight into `datetime`. It is your own shell, so this is a robustness rather than an attack finding — but the `eval` is unnecessary: the flags can be collected in an array and expanded safely. The function is also BSD-`date`-only (`-j`, `-v`, `-jf` at helpers.bash:40), which silently breaks on the Linux machines the installer half-supports, and `datetime.bats` cannot catch any of this because it tests a private copy (finding 13).

**Fix.** Build an array — `args=(); for m in ${mutator}; do args+=("-v${sign}${m}"); done; date -j "${args[@]}" +"${iso}"` — validate each `m` against `^[0-9]+[yMwdHmS]$` before use, and either gate the function on Darwin or add a `date --version` branch using GNU `date -d` syntax.
